overview: Two very different ways influenza changes its surface proteins — one gradual and predictable, the other sudden and pandemic-prone.

aspects.label: Overview / Core Definition
aspects.valueA: Gradual accumulation of small point mutations in the hemagglutinin/neuraminidase genes over time.
aspects.valueB: Sudden, major change in surface antigens caused by reassortment of gene segments between two different influenza strains co-infecting one host.

aspects.label: Mechanism
aspects.valueA: Point mutations accumulate due to the low-fidelity viral RNA polymerase.
aspects.valueB: Genetic reassortment of segmented RNA genome when two strains infect the same cell simultaneously.

aspects.label: Magnitude of Change
aspects.valueB: Large, abrupt antigenic change producing a novel subtype.

aspects.label: Virus Types Affected
aspects.valueA: Occurs in both influenza A and B.
aspects.valueB: Occurs only in influenza A, due to its segmented genome and animal reservoirs enabling co-infection and mixing.

aspects.label: Epidemiological Consequence
aspects.valueA: Responsible for seasonal influenza epidemics as immunity gradually wanes.
aspects.valueB: Responsible for influenza pandemics, since the population has little to no pre-existing immunity to the novel subtype.

aspects.label: Vaccine Implication
aspects.valueA: Necessitates yearly vaccine reformulation to match circulating strains.
aspects.valueB: Can render existing vaccines and immunity almost completely ineffective, requiring an entirely new vaccine.

overlay.memoryTrick: Drift = slow drift over time. Shift = a sudden shift to something new.
